As LDCs approach the midterm review of the Doha Programme of Action, this forum is more critical than ever. This serves as an urgent platform to address widening digital and AI divides that risk further enhancing entrenching global inequalities. LDCs are home to 1.22 billion people, nearly 60% of whom are under the age of 25. This is a powerful demographic force with the potential to drive science, technology, and innovation-led transformation at scale. However, realizing the opportunity demands decisive efforts to dismantle entrenched structural barriers and invest in inclusive, future-ready systems. Yet the digital foundation required for such transformation remains uneven. Even in 2024, only 35% of people had access to internet in LDCs, compared to 93% in high-income countries. They are constrained by high costs, uneven quality of access, persistent gender divide, and continued marginalization of rural communities. In this context, we would like to highlight several key issues. First, scaling up investment in digital and energy infrastructure is essential to ensure universal access to reliable electricity, affordable connectivity and secure digital public infrastructure. Second, targeted financing mechanisms and policy interventions are needed to reduce the cost of connectivity for inclusive digital transformation. Third, increasing investment in STEM education, research systems, and innovation ecosystems is key to building sustainable STI capacity. Strengthening human capital and research infrastructure is essential in enabling LDCs— for enabling LDCs to absorb and adapt to emerging technologies. Fourth, strengthening support for micro and small and medium enterprises, which are essential to create jobs and economic diversification in LDCs. Finally, stronger global partnership alongside increased and coordinated financing are essential to sustaining progress and preventing setbacks. We must ensure that LDCs do not miss out on rapid technological change, including advances in artificial intelligence. Excellencies, STI is fundamental to delivering on the promise of 2030 Agenda. Ensuring equitable access to technology, strengthening human capital, and mobilizing adequate financing are essential to leaving no one behind. I thank you.

Excellencies, distinguished participants, ladies and gentlemen, Good morning. It's a great honor for me to share with you the outcomes of the 29th Annual Session of the Commission on Science and Technology for Development, held from 20th to 24th April in Geneva, Switzerland. The Annual Session was well attended, with over 700 registered participants from 95 countries. At the Ministerial Roundtable aimed at contributing to this year's High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development, speakers who were mainly ministers and deputy ministers highlighted the role of STI in driving transformative, equitable, innovative, and coordinated actions for 2030 Agenda. We also examined the priority theme, Science, Technology, and Innovation in the Age of AI, to explore the transformative impact of AI on STI and the significant risks it entails. And more importantly, to support policymakers in developing countries to design responsible innovative policies to seize AI's benefits. Participants underscored the importance of capacity building and international cooperation to ensure that developing countries can effectively participate in and benefit from AI advancements. Particular attention was given to governance issues, including the need for agile and adaptive policy frameworks, ethical standards, and robust AI and data governance to address challenges such as digital divide and the concentration of technological power. Discussions on preparations for the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, scheduled for July 2026 in Geneva, further emphasized the importance of an inclusive, action-oriented process to foster convergence and synergy across existing initiatives. Speakers stressed that AI is not a neutral technology and that it trajectory will be shaped by policy choices, governance frameworks, and international cooperation. They called for greater investment in infrastructure, skills, and local innovation ecosystem, as well as strengthened international cooperation to ensure that AI is human-centered, inclusive, and well-governed, promoting sustainable and equitable development. CSD was recognized as a key platform in facilitating dialogue, coordination, and knowledge exchange on those issues, contributing to a more inclusive global AI ecosystem. Looking ahead, the 30th Annual Session of the CSDG, tentatively scheduled to take place from 19th to 23rd April 2027 in Geneva, will consider the priority theme Data Governance for Development: From Assembly to Equitable Stewardship. This will explore how equitable data governance can support shared prosperity and sustainable development. As usual, the intersessional panel will be held in November in Geneva as a key platform for strategic planning, sharing lessons learned and best practice in the STI field. We hope you can join us in the 30th Annual Session of the CSDD.
